Methodology: Quantitative computational project. First, the student will define a focused XR domain, inclusion criteria and structured extraction schema. Methodology: Participants perform computerised tasks requiring spatial and non-spatial forms of selective attention, while FEF, IFJ, and a control region are stimulated in different sessions using a theta-burst protocol that is known to transiently reduce neuronal excitability. Project title: Visual discomfort in autistic and non-autistic children and adults

Methodology: There are both in-person and online parts of this project, which students would be welcome to choose between, in discussion with the supervisor. In-person: we are seeing autistic and non-autistic children aged 6-14 years and finding out what they find comfortable or uncomfortable, and why. Children give visual discomfort ratings, and we will measure EEG and autonomic (ECG, pupillometry) responses. We are also seeing autistic and non-autistic adults, to compare which stimuli they find comfortable or uncomfortable to look at. Online: autistic and non-autistic adults and children judge whether a range of natural images are "comfortable" or "uncomfortable". We will then use image statistics (e.g., spatial frequency information, colour contrasts) to see if we can predict which images they find comfortable or not, and whether these predictions vary across autistic and non-autistic participants.
Skills & requirements: Tasks are already programmed. Programming skills will be helpful to preprocess and analyse the data, and extract image statistics from stimuli, however support will be provided. If you are interested in collecting in-person data with children, we require previous experience working with children, ideally including those with developmental conditions (in line with our ethics approval).
